n: Jehoash (Joash) begins his forty-year reign in Judah in Jehu’s seventh year (about 835 BC). His mother came from Beersheba in Judah’s far south.
He did right as long as Jehoiada the priest guided him. The phrase hints that his faithfulness depended on his mentor—Chronicles records that after Jehoiada died, Joash turned to idols.

f.w: wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him

n: The local hilltop shrines still operated, as under earlier good kings.
Joash orders the priests to collect all temple income: census money, assessed vows, and freewill gifts. The temple had been neglected or damaged under Athaliah.

f.w: every one that passeth the account
the money that every man is set at
f.g: money paid to redeem a vow, according to assessed value.

n: Each priest was to collect from his own contacts and use it to repair the damaged temple.

f.g: perhaps ‘assessor’ or ‘treasurer’; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

n: By the king’s twenty-third year, nothing had been repaired. The money had evidently gone elsewhere.
Joash confronts Jehoiada and the priests and changes the system: they must stop taking the money directly and turn it over for repairs.
The priests agree to stop collecting and also to give up responsibility for the repairs.
Jehoiada sets up a chest with a hole in the lid beside the altar. All offerings go straight into it—a simple, transparent system.
When the chest fills, the royal secretary and high priest count the money together and bag it. Two witnesses guard against mishandling sacred funds.
The money goes directly to the supervisors, who pay the carpenters and builders.
It also pays masons and stonecutters and buys timber and cut stone.
None of it was used for new decorative items; repairs came first.
All funds went to the workers and repairs.
The supervisors were so trustworthy that no one audited them. Faithful stewardship builds trust.
Money from guilt and sin offerings still went to support the priests, as the law provided.

f.g: payments connected with guilt and sin offerings.

n: Hazael of Aram captures Gath on the Philistine plain and turns toward Jerusalem.

f.g: a Philistine city southwest of Jerusalem.

n: To buy him off, Joash strips the temple and palace of all the treasures dedicated by himself and earlier kings. The temple he restored is now emptied to pay an enemy.
His other acts are recorded in Judah’s royal chronicles.
Joash’s own officials conspire and kill him at Beth-millo. Chronicles explains it as retribution for his murder of Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, who had rebuked him.

f.g: terraced fill or a fortification in Jerusalem.

n: The assassins are named, and Joash is buried in Jerusalem. His son Amaziah becomes king.
